title: Logical Placement
intro: Put each sentence where its ideas fit best.

sections.heading: Follow time and sequence cues
body: Use first, afterward, before, and similar cues to locate a sentence in the sequence. “Afterward, they cleaned” must follow the activity being cleaned up.
In a procedure, keep prerequisites before later steps: preheat before baking. Read both neighboring sentences to verify the order.

examples.text: [1] Mix the batter. [2] Pour it into the pan. [3] Bake until golden. 'Just before pouring, grease the pan.' goes before [2].
examples.label: 'just before pouring' anchors greasing to the pour

examples.text: 'Just before pouring, grease the pan.' placed after [3], the baking step.
examples.label: no one greases a pan after the cake has baked

sections.tip: Replay the events in real-world order. The sentence goes where its time word says it belongs.

sections.heading: Let cause come before effect
body: A sentence beginning “As a result” should follow the cause it refers to. Place needed definitions or explanations before a later sentence relies on them.
Check the actual connective. A writer can describe an effect before explaining its cause, but the chosen position must make that relationship clear.

examples.text: 'The valley was underwater by morning. A crack in the dam overnight explained the flooding.'
examples.label: Effect first, then a clearly signaled explanation: also coherent

examples.text: 'As a result, the valley was underwater. Only later does the paragraph introduce any cause.'
examples.label: A result connector needs an established cause to refer to

sections.tip: For a chronological cause-and-effect explanation, keep causes before results. Flashbacks can explain an effect afterward when the wording clearly signals the shift.

sections.heading: Use pronouns and references as anchors
body: Find the referent for it, they, this method, or these results. Those references usually point to an earlier introduction.
Test whether the proposed position makes the intended noun or idea clear. Reject a move that leaves the reference ambiguous or unsupported.

examples.text: 'Dr. Lee tested a new vaccine. It produced strong immunity.' ('It' = the vaccine, named first.)
examples.label: the noun appears before the pronoun

examples.text: 'It produced strong immunity. Dr. Lee tested a new vaccine.'
examples.label: 'It' has no earlier noun to point to

sections.tip: Find the intended referent and choose the position that makes it clear. An essay may already have introduced the noun in an earlier paragraph.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: When choices are positions, inspect the movable sentence for time cues, transitions, and references. Identify what each cue needs to connect to.
Read the preceding sentence, the moved sentence, and the following sentence together. Both links must work; a good connection on only one side is not enough.
sections.tip: The clue lives inside the movable sentence. Find its anchor before you look at the answer choices.

sections.heading: Advanced transfer: paragraph boundaries and transitions
body: A paragraph break should mark a change in the job the writing performs: for example, from explaining a method to evaluating its limitations. A new fact alone does not require a new paragraph.

For placement across paragraphs, test both links. A sentence may close the previous argument and introduce the next, so it needs to refer accurately backward while preparing the new focus. Follow rhetorical function as well as time.

examples.text: A paragraph explains how an archive scans maps. The next sentence begins, 'Access, however, posed a different problem: few residents had reliable internet.'
examples.label: A paragraph break before Access marks a shift from making digital copies to who can use them.

examples.text: Breaking after 'Access, however, posed a different problem' and before the explanation of that problem.
examples.label: That break separates the new topic from the explanation that develops it.

sections.tip: Label each paragraph’s job in a few words before testing a sentence position.

check.stem: [1] Spread the seeds evenly over the prepared soil. [2] Water them gently each morning. [3] [[First, loosen the top layer of soil with a rake.]] [4] Within two weeks, green shoots will appear.
check.questionText: For the sake of the logic of the paragraph, Sentence 3 should be placed:
check.explanation: 'First' marks raking as the opening step, and Sentence 1's 'the prepared soil' makes sense only after the soil has been loosened, so the sentence belongs before Sentence 1. 'Where it is now' puts raking after the seeds are planted and watered, 'after Sentence 1' loosens soil the seeds already cover, and 'after Sentence 4' puts preparation after the shoots have appeared.

check.stem: [1] In 1925, the town library occupied a single rented room. [2] Donations poured in after a local newspaper described the cramped conditions. [3] Within a decade, the collection had outgrown the new building as well. [4] [[The money paid for a brick building with space for ten thousand books.]]
check.questionText: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 4 should be placed:
check.explanation: 'The money' picks up the donations in Sentence 2, and Sentence 3's 'the new building' needs that brick building introduced first, so the sentence fits after Sentence 2. 'Where it is now' lets Sentence 3 mention 'the new building' before one exists, while 'before Sentence 1' and 'after Sentence 1' place 'the money' before any donations have been mentioned.

check.stem: [1] She sketched the design on graph paper. [2] She then cut the cedar panels to size. [3] Finally, she bolted the frame together. [4] [[Maria had always loved building things by hand.]]
check.questionText: For the sake of the logic and cohesion of the paragraph, Sentence 4 should be placed:
check.explanation: Sentence 1's 'She' needs Maria named first, so this background sentence must open the paragraph; before Sentence 1 is the only spot that supplies the name before the pronoun. 'Where it is now,' 'after Sentence 1,' and 'after Sentence 2' each leave at least one earlier 'She' with no named antecedent, and the last two also interrupt the sketch-cut-bolt sequence.
